If the fencer left during an attack, they return to where the attack started, then retreat one meter. Restoring the correct on-guard distance also matters.
A touch from this repositioning requires both feet beyond the rear line. A side exit by itself does not automatically give the opponent a point.
An involuntary exit caused by an accident, such as jostling, has an exception under t.36. Leaving to avoid a touch has a separate penalty.
questions: Where did the fencer leave the side?
Was the exit during an attack, and where did that attack start?
Would the required repositioning put both feet beyond the rear line?
Was there an accidental cause such as jostling?
cases.caveat: Touch validity during the exit is a separate question. One foot and both feet off have different rules; foil and sabre still apply their conventions.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: Passed the opponent, turned, and hit
cases.summary: Who passed whom matters. A hit made after passing by the fencer who went past is annulled. The opponent who was passed may make an immediate hit, even while turning.
conditions: The referee calls Halt as soon as a fencer goes completely past the opponent.
A touch made immediately as the passing happens can be valid. A later hit by the fencer who passed cannot.
The fencer who was passed may hit immediately, even while turning. This exception does not give either fencer unlimited time to start a new action.
Turning the back is separately prohibited. Foil and sabre also require their weapon conventions; sabre forbids the flèche and forward crossing of the feet.
questions: Which fencer went completely past the other?
Was the touch immediate as they passed, or made afterwards?
Was it the passing fencer or the fencer who was passed who hit?
Had a new action begun after Halt?
cases.caveat: The illustration shows the passing distinction only. It assumes no other fault and does not judge priority.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: The light came on, but the point hit the floor
cases.summary: A light is evidence of registration. A touch on the ground where it is not insulated is disregarded; an equipment fault is a separate route to annulment.
conditions: A foot is valid épée target. The floor is not the opponent. The referee must establish what was touched; the apparatus cannot identify the location.
If referee-supervised tests show a touch on the conductive strip registers a light, t.94.1 requires annulment of the last touch, subject to t.56.
If testing shows the strip is grounded and does not reproduce a fault, that test does not prove the original point landed on the foot or on the floor.
A fault need not repeat every time, but it must be demonstrated without doubt at least once during the supervised tests. Preserve the equipment and test immediately.

Check the event and the surface: the domestic Operations Manual permits local/division qualifier strips without grounding. A successful grounding test describes the tested setup; it does not determine where the earlier point landed.
questions: Did the referee establish a floor hit or a hit on the opponent?
Did a supervised test make a touch on the conductive strip register?
Was anything unplugged, adjusted or changed before testing?
Had fencing restarted before annulment was requested?
cases.caveat: Disagreeing with what the referee saw is a point-of-fact issue. Equipment tests or a specific misapplication of a rule raise different questions.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: My touch did not register — a plug was disconnected
cases.summary: The precise connection matters. An established equipment failure can justify cancelling the opponent’s last touch; an unplugged body cord has a specific exception.
conditions: A properly made touch that does not register can trigger t.94.2, subject to immediate supervised tests and the t.56 limits. A missing light cannot simply be converted into a point.
If the body cord is unplugged at the weapon or at the fencer’s back, that normally does not justify annulment.
At the back connection, a missing or nonfunctioning retaining safety device is an exception: t.95.1 says the touch should be annulled when that plug comes out.
A connecting cable unplugged at the reel or scoring apparatus is a different location. It needs the general equipment-failure tests; do not assume every unplugged connection is a body-cord exception.
A fencer who runs on after receiving a hit and tears out the reel or connecting line cannot use that later disconnection to annul the hit under t.28.3.
questions: Which plug came out: weapon, fencer’s back, reel, or apparatus?
If at the back, was the retaining safety device present and working?
Was the failure established in immediate referee-supervised tests?
Was the connection lost during the action or after the registered touch?
Was the fencer disadvantaged by the failure, and has fencing restarted?
cases.caveat: Annulment cancels a registered touch. It does not award an unregistered touch or recreate an assumed double.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: Both lights came on — does each fencer score?
cases.summary: In épée, two registered valid touches give each fencer a touch. Both lights alone do not override rules that make one touch invalid.
conditions: The whole body, clothing and equipment are target in épée. Hits must still satisfy the validity rules.
If one registered touch is valid and the other is invalid, only the valid touch scores. Equipment-failure doubles have their own treatment in t.94.5.
If a fencer is completely off the side with both feet, only the opponent remaining on the strip with at least one foot can have a valid hit under t.33.4.
At 4–4 in a five-touch pool, and during the deciding extra minute, explicit USA exceptions exclude doubles. Check the score and phase before applying the ordinary rule.
At 14–14 in the standard 15-touch DE finishing situation, a double does not count; see the dedicated entry and its source distinction.
questions: Did the apparatus register both touches?
Were both touches valid, rather than a floor hit, late hit or boundary exception?
cases.caveat: An ordinary double can score both. Pool 4–4, regulation DE 14–14 and the deciding extra minute have finishing/tie exceptions; adapted formats need their own provisions.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: A touch landed after “Halt”
cases.summary: After Halt, no new action may start. A movement already begun may remain valid, but other stopping rules can still invalidate the touch.
conditions: Check when the action began, rather than only when the light appeared.
Passing, leaving the strip and other specific rules can annul a touch even if the action began before Halt.
A fencer who stops before the referee calls Halt can still receive a valid touch.
questions: Did the movement begin before Halt?
Was there a specific stop condition, such as passing or leaving the strip?
cases.caveat: Expiration of fencing time is a separate cutoff under t.44. Do not apply the already-started movement exception to the final buzzer.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: A white light came on in foil
cases.summary: A normal off-target foil touch does not score, but it stops the phrase and annuls touches made afterwards.
conditions: Only touches on valid foil target count. A normal hit to the arm, leg or head is off target.
The off-target touch stops the phrase; the order of the touches matters.
Covering or substituting non-valid target has special rules in t.79. This entry describes an ordinary off-target touch.
questions: Was the light an ordinary off-target indication?
Did the other touch arrive before or after the off-target touch?
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: Two colored lights in foil — who scores?
cases.summary: Foil applies its conventions to decide validity and priority. Two colored lights do not give a point to each fencer.
conditions: The referee analyzes the fencing phrase and applies the foil conventions, including attack, parry and riposte.
Lights establish registration; the referee still decides which touch is valid under those conventions.
This first collection explains why priority matters. It does not yet break down every attack and counterattack case.
questions: What phrase did the referee describe?
Is the question about their observation, or a specific rule applied to that observation?
cases.caveat: Open the official foil conventions t.83–89 for the full priority rules.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: Two lights in sabre — who scores?
cases.summary: Sabre applies its conventions to decide validity and priority. Two lights do not give a point to each fencer.
conditions: The referee analyzes the fencing phrase and applies the sabre conventions.
The apparatus records touches; it does not decide attack, parry, riposte or priority.
This first collection explains why priority matters. It does not yet break down every attack and counterattack case.
questions: What phrase did the referee describe?
Is the question about their observation, or a specific rule applied to that observation?
cases.caveat: Open the official sabre conventions t.101–106 for the full priority rules.
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: A sabre hit landed on the leg
cases.summary: An ordinary sabre touch off target does not score, does not register, and does not stop the phrase.
conditions: The ordinary off-target rule is different from foil’s white-light stop.
Other rules, such as a fencing fault or going completely off the side, may still stop the phrase and invalidate subsequent touches.
questions: Was the hit off target, with no other stopping condition?
cases.review_note: Vocabulary describes ways to find this situation; it does not establish facts or decide the call.

cases.title: Crossed the rear line — one foot or both?
cases.summary: Crossing the rear limit completely, with both feet, awards a touch against the fencer who went off. One foot alone is not that automatic rear-exit touch.
conditions: t.34 requires both feet completely beyond the rear limit. Identify the actual line, not the end of conductive runoff.
An involuntary boundary crossing caused by an accident, such as jostling, has the t.36 exception.
A side exit can lead to a rear-line touch after the required retreat; that is a separate repositioning route.
questions: Were both feet completely beyond the rear line?
Was there an accidental cause, such as jostling?
Was this a rear exit or a side-exit retreat?
cases.caveat: The boundary touch does not settle every accompanying action. Check timing and other applicable faults.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: Hit while leaving the side — can it count?
cases.summary: One foot off and both feet off have different touch-validity rules. For épée, after both feet leave, only the fencer still on the strip can score with a simple immediate action.
conditions: The referee calls Halt once one or both feet are completely off the side.
With only one foot off, the departing fencer’s touch can be valid if the action started before Halt.
With both feet off, the departing fencer’s later actions are annulled. A received touch can still count if it results from a simple, immediate action.
For épée, only the opponent remaining with at least one foot on the strip can score in that situation, even with two lights. Foil and sabre still apply their conventions.
questions: Was one foot off or were both feet off?
When did the action start relative to Halt?
Which fencer made the touch?
Was the received action simple and immediate?
cases.caveat: The ground lost after a side exit is a separate question from validity of the touch.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: A touch during or after a fall
cases.summary: t.56.10 requires annulment of a touch made during or after a fall. A touch already made before the fall is a different timing question.
conditions: Identify when the touch was made relative to the fall, rather than assuming the light alone establishes the sequence.
An already-started action after an ordinary Halt does not override the specific fall rule.
Ask the referee to explain the observed sequence; disagreement about that sequence is a point-of-fact issue.
questions: Was the touch before, during or after the fall?
What sequence did the referee establish?
cases.caveat: This entry explains touch validity, not injury treatment or every penalty for an abnormal action.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: My blade broke and the opponent scored
cases.summary: If the fencer who received the registered touch has a broken blade, annulment is required unless the break clearly happened after registration.
conditions: t.56.7 applies to the fencer against whom the touch was registered.
A break clearly after registration does not cancel that touch under this clause.
Preserve the equipment and request immediate referee-supervised examination. The general t.56 timing and preservation limits still matter.
Annulment cancels the opponent’s touch; it does not award an unregistered hit.
questions: Whose blade broke?
Did it clearly break after the touch registered?
Was the setup preserved and has fencing restarted?
cases.caveat: A broken blade on the other side is not automatically the same annulment situation.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: It only failed once during the equipment test
cases.summary: A fault does not have to repeat on every test. It must appear without doubt at least once during referee-supervised testing.
conditions: Keep the equipment unchanged and test immediately after the stop.
Only the last touch is eligible, and only if the fencer who received it was disadvantaged by the failure.
Use the specific annulment conditions for the selected weapon; a demonstrated fault is not automatically a point for the testing fencer.
Repeated abnormal registrations require expert examination under t.56.8–9, with nothing altered before the check.
questions: Was a fault demonstrated without doubt in supervised tests?
Which fencer was disadvantaged?
Was anything changed, or had fencing restarted?
cases.caveat: A normal test does not prove where a previous point landed or reconstruct an unregistered touch.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: Épée light from a beat or movement, without a hit
cases.summary: A demonstrated spurious registration can require annulment of the opponent’s last touch. The fault must be established under the supervised-test rules.
conditions: t.94.3 covers a light against the disadvantaged fencer from a beat, opponent movement, or another cause that is not a properly made touch.
t.94.4 separately covers a fencer’s registration being cancelled by the opponent’s subsequent touch.
Preserve the setup and test immediately; the general last-touch and no-restart limits apply.
questions: Did supervised tests demonstrate a light without a proper touch?
Was one registration suppressed by a subsequent touch?
Was the receiving fencer disadvantaged?
cases.caveat: This is an épée equipment rule. Foil and sabre have different annulment lists.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: An épée guard lights up, but it has paint or oxidation
cases.summary: A guard or conductive-strip hit registering can support annulment, but t.94.1 excludes insulation on the épée and a tip that can be tightened or unscrewed by hand.
conditions: The general guard/strip registration condition and its stated equipment exceptions must be read together.
Oxidation, glue, paint or other insulating material on the receiving fencer’s épée cannot justify annulment of touches against that fencer.
The same clause excludes a badly fixed tip that can be unscrewed or tightened by hand.
Do not adjust the tip or clean the guard before the referee decides; testing and preservation still matter.
questions: What surface caused the test light?
Was insulation, paint, glue or oxidation on the épée involved?
Was the tip loose enough to turn by hand?
cases.caveat: An excluded reason for annulment does not make the equipment compliant or settle any separate equipment penalty.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: The point tore the conductive strip and a light appeared
cases.summary: If a ground touch tears the conductive strip and at the same time registers against the opponent, t.95.2 requires annulment.
conditions: The rule describes tearing the strip with a touch on the ground, together with a registration against the opponent.
Establish that sequence; not every damaged area or floor light proves this happened.
Preserve the setup and raise the issue immediately under the general t.56 limits.
questions: Did the point tear the conductive strip?
Did a light against the opponent register at the same time?
cases.caveat: A floor touch without this tearing sequence is covered by the ordinary ground-touch and equipment rules.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: One épée touch is established and the other is doubtful
cases.summary: t.94.5 distinguishes a known invalid touch from a doubtful touch caused by apparatus failure. An established/doubtful double has a specific choice for the fencer who made the established touch.
conditions: With one valid and one invalid touch, only the valid touch is scored.
With one established touch and one doubtful touch due to apparatus failure, the fencer who made the established touch may accept the double or ask to have it annulled.
Do not turn an observed invalid floor touch into the different apparatus-failure situation.
Any equipment annulment must respect the general testing and preservation requirements.
questions: Is the second touch known invalid or doubtful because of an apparatus failure?
Which fencer made the established touch?
What choice did that fencer make?
cases.caveat: This provision does not let either fencer cancel any ordinary double they dislike.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: Épée pool at 4–4 — why did the double not count?
cases.summary: In an ordinary five-touch épée pool bout at 4–4, double touches do not count. The fencers keep their positions and fence for a deciding touch up to the time limit.
conditions: t.38.1.b supplies the explicit exception to the usual épée double rule.
The score stays 4–4 after a double, and the fencers retain their positions.
If time expires tied, the deciding extra minute has its own drawn-priority procedure and also excludes doubles.
questions: Is this a five-touch pool bout?
Was the score 4–4?
Was this regulation time or the extra minute?
cases.caveat: This entry does not establish a finishing-double rule for DE bouts or modified formats.
cases.review_note: Reviewed retrieval terms describe a situation, not a ruling. Check the weapon, facts and stated scope.

cases.title: Tied when time expires — priority and the extra minute
cases.summary: A tied bout goes to a deciding touch with a maximum extra minute. Lots are drawn first to choose the winner if the tie remains at the end.
conditions: The ordinary pool and DE rules describe a deciding touch, not an extra minute that must always run in full.
Drawn priority is the fallback winner if the score remains tied; it is different from foil/sabre priority in a fencing phrase.

A conductive surface can prevent an otherwise expected registration; equipment compliance and touch annulment remain separate questions.
Preserve the setup and let the referee determine any demonstrated fault and its applicable annulment rule.
questions: Does the mask have a conductive foil/sabre bib?
Which weapon and event are being fenced?
Was a non-registration fault established?
cases.caveat: Do not infer that every mask touch without a light is this fault.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Electrical timing — why one light instead of two?
cases.summary: Each weapon has a different apparatus timing specification. The electrical registration window is not foil/sabre priority or one universal definition of simultaneous fencing actions.
conditions: Épée: below 40 ms both touches must register; above 50 ms only the first must register. The apparatus tolerance lies between those limits.
Foil: subsequent signals are ignored after 300 ms, with ±25 ms tolerance. Appendix B explicitly separates this from fencing time.
Sabre: the subsequent touch has a maximum delay of 170 ms, with ±10 ms tolerance.
Whether a registered touch is valid still depends on target, timing, boundaries and the weapon’s conventions.
questions: Which weapon mode was selected?
Is the question electrical registration or priority?
Was an apparatus fault demonstrated?
cases.caveat: Do not use one exact épée cutoff or infer priority from which lamp appeared first.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: The grounded surface extends beyond the fencing strip
cases.summary: A conductive runoff or safety border is not automatically legal combat area. Electrical grounding and the marked boundaries answer different questions.
conditions: t.18.3 says conductive safety borders do not form part of the strip.
m.57 describes conductive extensions that neutralize ground touches and allow retreat beyond the rear limits.
Use the actual rear and side markings for boundary decisions.
Domestic local/division competitions may have different strip dimensions and grounding requirements.
questions: Where are the marked rear and side limits?
Was the contact on combat area or conductive runoff?
Which domestic event-level strip requirements apply?
cases.caveat: A successful grounding test does not establish where an earlier hit landed.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: A point was added without a physical hit
cases.summary: Boundary and penalty touches can change the score without an ordinary registered physical hit. They are explicit exceptions to the usual registration requirement.
conditions: t.54.2 expressly recognizes penalty touches and the foil t.79 exception.
Crossing the rear boundary completely or a required side-exit retreat can award a boundary touch.
A red penalty touch and cancellation of the offender’s physical touch are separate consequences.
Use the penalty companion for the card group, earlier offenses, current passivity rules and exclusions.
questions: Was the point a physical registration, boundary touch or penalty?
What rule or card was announced?
Was an offender’s physical touch also annulled?
cases.caveat: A missing physical registration is not converted into a point merely because penalty exceptions exist.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: The final hit is scored — is the bout finished?
cases.summary: The final registered hit and formal completion are different. Raise any eligible immediate review before unhooking or continuing; do not assume a finished bout can be restarted.
conditions: t.122 describes the final decision and required salutes; completion is not simply seeing the final light.
t.37.3 prohibits restarting the same bout or relay after it is finished, even for a formal mistake.
The domestic on-strip protest deadline ends once the fencer unhooks or fences another touch.
A scoresheet correction follows its own handbook procedure; it is not a blanket right to reopen touch decisions.
questions: Has the referee given the final decision?
Was an eligible review raised immediately while still hooked up?
Is the concern a touch decision or a recorded-score error?
cases.caveat: The October handshake overlay is handled in the penalty companion; the historical t.122 wording is not a substitute for that current audit.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Same number of pool wins — why am I seeded lower?
cases.summary: Pool ranking first compares victories divided by bouts, then touches scored minus touches received, then total touches scored. Absolute equality is resolved by lots under o.73.
conditions: Compare victory ratio, rather than raw victory count when numbers of bouts differ.
The indicator is touches scored minus touches received.
If ratios and indicators match, more touches scored ranks higher.
The event’s domestic format controls promotion. Do not infer qualification from ranking alone or transfer every international cutoff provision.
questions: Did both fencers fence the same number of bouts?
What are the victory ratios, indicators and touches scored?
Which event’s promotion rule applies?
cases.caveat: A recording error should be raised during the scoresheet review period.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Foil hit white because valid target was covered
cases.summary: Foil target substitution can override the ordinary off-target result. t.79 can award a correctly given touch registered off-target because valid target was protected or substituted.
conditions: The offender’s own touch is annulled and a first-group penalty applies.
t.79.1.b covers a correctly given touch registering non-valid because valid surface was protected/substituted.
t.79.1.c addresses off-target hits when an abnormal position substituted non-valid target for valid target.
The referee determines whether this happened; a white light alone does not establish covering.
questions: Was valid target protected or substituted?
Did that cause the correctly given touch to register white?
What facts did the referee establish?
cases.caveat: The ordinary white-light case remains different when there is no established substitution.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Sabre touched target and the blade, or whipped around a parry
cases.summary: A through-blade hit is valid when it clearly arrives on target. A properly executed sabre parry is judged as a parry even if blade flexibility lets the tip contact target.
conditions: t.96.4 concerns simultaneous contact with target and the opponent’s sabre.
t.105.2 defines a parry by preventing arrival before completion through closing the relevant line.
Do not classify a whip-over, failed parry and clear through-blade target hit as one identical action.
Apparatus suppression of whip-over signals is a material specification, not an automatic priority ruling.
questions: Did the hit clearly arrive on valid target?
Was the attack properly parried before completion?
Was the contact a result of blade flexibility?
cases.caveat: The referee establishes the parry and contact sequence.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: The wrong team fencers fenced the relay
cases.summary: o.99.3 says an altered relay order cancels all touches scored since the modification, whether intentional or accidental, and the match resumes in the correct order.
conditions: Identify the first point at which the prescribed order changed.
A requested reserve substitution is a separate process with announcement and timing requirements.
Medical replacement during a relay has a different provision from ordinary between-bout substitution.
Have the referee and Bout Committee check the team sheet; the guide does not infer the correct roster from names alone.
questions: Which relay order was prescribed?
When did the deviation begin?
Was a properly announced substitution or medical replacement involved?
cases.caveat: International-specific organizational requirements in o.99 must retain their stated event scope.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Attack, parry, riposte, remise — what do the words mean?
cases.summary: These names describe actions in a fencing phrase. Knowing the definitions helps understand a call; it does not establish which action actually occurred.
conditions: An attack is the initial offensive action; a riposte follows a parry, and a counter-riposte follows a parry of a riposte.
A parry is a defensive weapon action preventing an offensive action from arriving.
A counterattack is made during the opponent’s offensive action.
Remise, redoublement and reprise describe different renewals in t.13. Electrical lockout is not the convention’s fencing time.
Épée uses these action terms descriptively; they do not create foil/sabre right-of-way in épée. Fencing time in t.8 is the time needed for one simple action, distinct from effective bout-clock time.
questions: Which action did the referee identify?
Was an attack parried, avoided or renewed?
Is electrical registration being confused with fencing time?
cases.caveat: This covers written definitions. Current borderline visual classification remains for the referee.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Foil attack or preparation — the written distinctions
cases.summary: The foil conventions distinguish a correctly executed attack from preparation using extension, target threat and the timing of advance, lunge or flèche.
conditions: t.83 distinguishes simple, compound and advance-lunge/advance-flèche attacks.
The simple attack’s extension and threat precede initiation of the lunge or flèche.
A compound attack presents the first feint with extending arm and threat, without bending between its successive actions and the launch.
The written bent-arm preparation provision is not a license for this app to grade an observed video or decide a borderline call.
questions: Was the action simple, compound or advance-lunge?
What extension and threat did the referee establish?
When did the final action launch?
cases.caveat: Use established facts and the event referee’s analysis. The guide does not provide a current visual interpretation certification.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Sabre attack, preparation and forward crossing
cases.summary: Sabre’s written attack conditions consider extension, continuous threat and touch timing relative to the front foot. Forward crossing of the rear foot past the front foot is separately prohibited.
conditions: t.101 distinguishes simple/compound lunge and advance-lunge attacks.
Its lunge provisions require the touch no later than the front foot contacting the strip.
t.101.5 prohibits the flèche and forward crossing and cancels the offender’s touch; the opponent’s correctly executed touch remains valid.
A current borderline attack/preparation call requires the referee’s assessment of the full phrase.
questions: What attack form did the referee identify?
What were the extension, threat and arrival sequence?
Did the rear foot completely pass the front foot in forward movement?
cases.caveat: This is the written framework, not an automatic reading of arm or foot positions.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: A straight-arm point in line was already there
cases.summary: A point in line continuously threatens valid target with a straight sword arm. If it is already established when an attack begins, the attacker must first deflect the blade.
conditions: t.15 defines the position; merely pointing or straightening the arm does not prove every condition.
Foil t.84 and sabre t.102 require deflection of an existing line; a mere graze is not enough.
If the attempt to find the blade fails through dérobement, the written right of attack passes to the opponent.
A line established later in an existing attack is a different timing situation.
questions: Was a continuous valid-target line established before the attack began?
Was it actually deflected or merely grazed?
Did the search for the blade fail?
cases.caveat: The referee establishes line timing, continuity and deflection.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Beat near the guard versus the tip end
cases.summary: The written conventions distinguish a beat on the opponent’s foible from one on the forte. Beat location can change who has the right to the immediate next action.
conditions: Foible is the two-thirds furthest from the guard; forte is the one-third nearest the guard.
A correctly executed beat attack on the foible retains priority under foil t.85 and sabre t.104.
A beat on the forte is badly executed and gives the opponent the right to an immediate riposte.
Any blade contact is not automatically a beat, parry or sufficient line deflection.
questions: Where on the blade was contact?
Was it a beat attack or a parry?
Was the resulting riposte immediate?
cases.caveat: This requires an established contact location and action classification.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Parried, then paused — does the riposte still have priority?
cases.summary: A parry gives the right to riposte, but the simple riposte must be immediate to annul the attacker’s subsequent action. A pause can permit renewal of the attack.
conditions: Foil t.86 and sabre t.105 require no indecision, hesitation or delay for the stated simple-riposte protection.
The judging clauses distinguish an immediate riposte from a pause allowing remise, redoublement or reprise.
Finding the blade during a compound attack can create a riposte opportunity under t.87/t.103.
Apparatus timing alone does not establish immediacy in the fencing phrase.
questions: Was the original attack properly parried?
Was the riposte immediate or delayed?
Did the attacker renew before that delayed response?
cases.caveat: The full sequence and weapon conventions matter; a parry is not permanent priority.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: A counterattack during a compound attack
cases.summary: For the written in-time stop-hit condition against a compound attack, the stop hit must arrive before the attacker begins the final movement, separated by a period of fencing time.
conditions: Foil t.88 and sabre t.103.3 give that condition.
A stop hit into a simple attack is not the same exception.
The judging articles distinguish a stop hit in time, a stop hit too late, and an attacker’s pause during a compound action.
The 300 ms/170 ms electrical windows are not the convention’s fencing time.
questions: Was the attack simple or compound?
When did the final movement begin?
Did the attacker pause and what sequence did the referee establish?
cases.caveat: This entry states the written timing condition; it cannot determine the observed interval.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Both attacked together — why no point?
cases.summary: The conventions distinguish simultaneous conception/execution of attacks from two lights caused by one fencer’s faulty action. Simultaneous attacks annul both touches.
conditions: Foil t.89.2 and sabre t.106.1 describe simultaneous attacks.
For foil, that simultaneous-action clause annuls both even if one touch was off-target.
An actual coup double instead requires analysis of the fault and priority; two lights alone do not distinguish these cases.
If the referee cannot clearly determine which side committed the fault, the conventions require replacement on guard.
questions: Did the referee identify simultaneous attacks or a fault in one action?
Were both conception and execution judged simultaneous?
Was a priority sequence established?
cases.caveat: The app does not choose a winner from two lamps or two moving fencers.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: An injury pause or medical withdrawal during the bout
cases.summary: A medical pause is an official procedure under t.45, not an automatic replay. The designated sports medicine professional determines treatment time and whether the fencer can continue.
conditions: The attested break is no longer than five minutes, timed from the professional’s opinion and reserved for treatment.
A further break the same day requires a different injury or medical reason.
If the professional finds the fencer incapable of continuing, individual withdrawal or a permitted team replacement applies.
Ask the event officials to follow the medical procedure; this entry gives no diagnosis or treatment advice.
questions: Was the medical reason attested by the designated professional?
Is this individual or team fencing?
Was withdrawal or replacement required?
cases.caveat: Medical decisions, ratings and qualification consequences are distinct from replaying a touch.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: Withdrawal, exclusion and the recorded result
cases.summary: Not completing a bout, medically withdrawing, and being excluded are different outcomes. Domestic medical-withdrawal results depend on whether the pool was completed.
conditions: o.79 declares the opponent the winner when a fencer cannot start or complete the bout.
The domestic handbook says an incomplete-pool medical withdrawal has no results to report for field rating/qualification calculations.
After completed pools or during DE, the handbook preserves the place for its stated results calculations.
Ordinary exclusion and current passivity loss have distinct consequences; use the penalty companion and ask the Bout Committee for the exact classification.
questions: Was this medical withdrawal, ordinary exclusion or a passivity loss?
Was the pool completed?
Is the question bout outcome, final place, rating or qualification?
cases.caveat: This is not a rating or qualification calculator, and the historical handbook’s old article numbers are not silently treated as current citations.
cases.review_note: Reviewed reference entry. Its stated facts and scope must be established; it does not decide the action.

cases.title: No touch for a minute — October 2026 non-combativity
cases.summary: From October 1, 2026, the first qualifying minute without a touch brings simultaneous P-red; the second occurrence brings P-black under the score/initial-seeding rule. Individual DE and team scopes differ.
conditions: Effective October 1, 2026; do not apply this revised sequence to an earlier event.
Individual DE: First occurrence: both fencers receive P-red. Each opponent gains one penalty touch; fencing continues.
Individual DE: Second occurrence: the lower-scoring fencer receives P-black and loses the bout. At a tie, the fencer with the lower initial seeding loses.
Teams: First occurrence: both teams receive P-red together. Each opponent gains one penalty touch; the relay continues.
Teams: Second occurrence in the match: the lower-scoring team receives P-black and loses the match. At a tie, the team with the lower initial seeding loses.
Individual: this procedure applies to direct elimination, not pools. Team: P-card history carries across all nine relays in the match.

The minute restarts after a touch, an off-target or annulled touch, a penalty touch, and at the start of each period or relay. P-cards are separate from ordinary cards and expire after the bout or match.
No P-card is awarded at 14–14 individually or 44–44 in a team match. If time runs out with a tied score, use the normal tie-breaking procedure instead.
Initial seeding means the competition’s starting order, not the score in this bout. Check the event’s official seeding; the FIE text bases its order on FIE ranking.
questions: Is the event on or after October 1, 2026?
Is this individual DE or a team match?
Which qualifying occurrence is this?
What are the scores and official initial seedings?
cases.caveat: This entry reuses the completed update audit. It does not mix ordinary yellow/red histories with P-cards or extend individual DE non-combativity to pools.
cases.review_note: Current guidance derives from the already completed domestic-adoption audit.

cases.title: Started or touched before “Fence”
cases.summary: No movement made or initiated before the command Fence is counted. A light appearing later does not validate an action that began too early.
conditions: t.23.1 uses the start of the movement, not merely the time the light appeared.
The ready question and on-guard command do not authorize fencing.
The ordinary already-started movement exception after Halt does not authorize actions started before Fence.
questions: When did the movement begin?
Had the referee given Fence?
cases.caveat: Any separate penalty for anticipation must be assessed under its own provision.
cases.review_note: Bounded reference; establish the facts and event scope.

cases.title: Absolute tie for the final national-qualifier slot
cases.summary: The domestic handbook’s national-qualifier provision requires a fence-off for an absolute tie at the final qualifying slot. That is a different question from ordinary pool seeding.
conditions: The provision applies to the national-qualifier formats identified in the handbook, not every tournament ranking.
The handbook specifies a 15-touch fence-off or the DE format required for the event’s age level.
Do not apply the general international pool cutoff clause without checking this domestic qualifier exception.
Ask the Bout Committee to identify the exact tied slot, format and qualifying-event rule.
questions: Is this a covered national qualifier?
Is the tie absolute at the final qualifying slot?
What DE format applies to the age category?
cases.caveat: A tie in an earlier ranking criterion is not necessarily an absolute tie.
cases.review_note: Bounded reference; establish the facts and event scope.

cases.title: Two hands, switching hands, or sliding the grip
cases.summary: The weapon is used with one hand only. Changing hands before the bout ends requires special referee permission for a hand/arm injury; grip position has its own restrictions.
conditions: t.21.4 is the one-hand and injury-permission rule.
With a plain handle, hand position can change during a bout, but it may not slip from front to back during an offensive action.
The weapon cannot become a throwing weapon; the hand must not leave the grip in its use.
Special/orthopedic handles have orientation requirements in t.21.3.
questions: Was a second hand used or the weapon hand changed?
Was injury permission given?
Did the grip slide during the offensive action?
cases.caveat: Grip position and prohibited free-hand offensive/defensive use are different questions.
cases.review_note: Apply the cited conditions to facts established by the referee.

cases.title: Restoring distance after Halt or body contact
cases.summary: Ordinary Halt preserves ground gained until a touch is awarded, with equal retreat to restore fencing distance. A fencer subjected to body contact or a flèche has a specific position-preservation provision.
conditions: t.31 describes equal retreat for ordinary restoration of fencing distance.
t.32 preserves the previously occupied place of the fencer subjected to corps à corps or a flèche.
t.22.8 prevents ordinary correct-distance replacement pushing behind the rear line a fencer who was in front when halted; an already rear-line foot remains as specified.
A lateral exit has the separate t.22.9 rule, which can produce a rear-line boundary touch.
questions: Why did the referee stop the bout?
Which fencer was subjected to the contact or flèche?
Was there a lateral exit or an ordinary distance restoration?
cases.caveat: Do not apply the ordinary distance rule over the side-exit or passing exceptions.
cases.review_note: Apply the cited conditions to facts established by the referee.

cases.title: Can judges help with floor hits, boundaries or free-hand use?
cases.summary: t.48 allows judges to assist the referee with observations including épée floor hits, exits, free-hand use and target substitution. Their role is official assistance, not a spectator vote.
conditions: The referee remains responsible for the decision with the apparatus and official assistance.
t.30 separately permits two neutral judges for free-hand or target-covering concerns, designated by the Head Referee.
Ask the event officials about the appropriate assistance and any applicable finals requirements.
Appointing judges does not retroactively establish that an earlier point hit the floor.
questions: What observation needs assistance?
Were official judges appointed?
What facts did the referee establish?
cases.caveat: The guide does not create a universal right to demand a replay or choose your own judges.
cases.review_note: Apply the cited conditions to facts established by the referee.

cases.title: Can I ask for a fuller explanation of the phrase?
cases.summary: Yes. The notes to t.63 expressly allow fencers to ask politely for a more complete analysis. Asking for explanation is distinct from a formal appeal.
conditions: Ask which sequence the referee found and which rule was applied.
An ordinary appeal cannot challenge a point of fact; a definite rule-application issue has its own immediate route.
Official video and equipment tests have separate requester, timing and preservation requirements.
questions: Do you need an explanation, a test, official video, or a rule-application protest?
What facts and rule did the referee identify?
cases.caveat: A request for explanation does not extend the deadline for any formal procedure.
cases.review_note: Apply the cited conditions to facts established by the referee.

cases.title: Deliberately made a light on the floor or another object
cases.summary: Intentionally causing registration by putting the point on the ground or a surface other than the opponent is a second-group offense under t.55.2. That differs from an accidental object hit or apparatus fault.
conditions: The false object registration is disregarded under t.55.1.
Intentional causing of the signal must be established; a floor light alone does not prove intent.
The second-group penalty is a red penalty touch; other validity questions remain distinct.
questions: What was hit?
Did the referee establish intentional false registration or an accidental contact?
Was a fault demonstrated?
cases.caveat: Do not classify every surprising light as cheating.
cases.review_note: Apply the cited conditions to facts established by the referee.
